title: Predicate Phrases
storyTitle: Action Blueprints at the Detective Agency

steps.settingDescription: Large chalk diagrams on Detective Ira's wall split every clue sentence into two halves: Subject on the left, and the entire Predicate Phrase on the right.

dialogues.line: Wait! I thought 'Predicate' meant ONLY the verb! Why did you underline TEN words after 'The messenger'?
In 'The messenger quietly handed Maharaj Vakya a sealed parcel at dawn', 'The messenger' is the Subject—and EVERYTHING from the finite verb onwards is the Predicate Phrase!
Inside that Predicate Phrase, the main verb acts like a strict architect: some verbs forbid objects ('slept'), some demand one or two objects ('handed'), and some demand complements ('became')!
Let us map out all the core Predicate Phrase blueprints so no verb ever loses its required companions.

steps.storyCallout: Goal: Break Predicate Phrases into verb groups, objects, complements, and optional adjuncts across standard clause patterns.

steps.subtopicTitle: Verb Group + Required Complements vs. Optional Adjuncts
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: If a sentence is a two-piece bicycle, the Subject is the front wheel and the PREDICATE PHRASE is the entire back half—pedals (Verb), mandatory cargo rack (Objects / Complements), and optional bell or streamers (Adjuncts)!
steps.formalDefinition: The predicate phrase (or verb phrase at clause level) comprises the finite verb group together with all elements governed by or modifying it: direct and indirect objects, subject or object complements, and adverbial adjuncts.
steps.simpleExplanation:
Every Predicate Phrase starts with its Verb Group. What comes NEXT depends on the verb:
1) Mandatory Elements (must stay or the sentence breaks): Direct Object ('She broke the seal'), Indirect + Direct Object ('He gave me a map'), Subject Complement ('The clue looks genuine'), Object Complement ('We elected Riya captain'), or Obligatory Place Adverbial ('Put the key on the desk'—you can't stop at *Put the key!).
2) Optional Adjuncts (can be removed cleanly): Extra time, place, or manner details ('early in the morning', 'carefully').
Note: Fronted adverbs ('Yesterday, she arrived') still belong functionally to the predicate even when moved to the front for emphasis.

structurePatterns.formName: Predicate = Verb + Required Parts + Optional Adjuncts
structurePatterns.sample: Ira [inspected] [the footprints] (with a magnifying glass at noon).

structurePatterns.formula: SV (Birds fly) | SVC (Milk tastes sweet) | SVO (Kiran solved the puzzle)
structurePatterns.sample: Note: In 'She became a pilot', 'a pilot' is a Complement (renames 'She'), NOT an Object!

realLifeExamples.sentence: The clever watchmaker repaired the broken pendulum within two hours.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Predicate Phrase = 'repaired (V) + the broken pendulum (DO) + within two hours (Optional Time Adjunct)'.

realLifeExamples.sentence: Keep your umbrella beside the door.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: 'Beside the door' is OBLIGATORY after 'keep/put' here—removing it leaves *Keep your umbrella (different/incomplete sense).

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: Chikoo placed the golden key carefully.
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: Chikoo placed the golden key carefully inside the drawer.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: Verbs of placement like 'put' and 'place' require a destination/location phrase inside the predicate, not just a manner adverb.

exceptions: Passivising an SVO sentence promotes the Direct Object to Subject and turns the original Subject into an optional 'by'-adjunct ('The puzzle was solved by Kiran').

steps.stepTitle: Checkpoint 1: Mark the Complete Predicate Phrase
steps.storyPrompt: Detective Ira underlines the Subject in: "All the Grade IX explorers quickly mapped the canyon before dusk."
steps.questionPrompt: Which span makes up the COMPLETE Predicate Phrase?
options: quickly mapped the canyon before dusk
acceptedAnswers: quickly mapped the canyon before dusk
steps.hint: Once you set aside the full Subject Noun Phrase ('All the Grade IX explorers'), EVERYTHING else—including 'quickly' and 'before dusk'—forms the Predicate Phrase!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Detective Ira: "Exact! Every word outside the subject ('quickly mapped the canyon before dusk') belongs to the Predicate Phrase."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Select the span containing the adverb 'quickly', the verb 'mapped', the object, and the time adjunct.

feedbackWrongByOption.mapped the canyon: Don't drop the manner adverb 'quickly' or the time adjunct 'before dusk'!

steps.simplerExample: In 'Our school team | practised steadily after class', the second half is the full Predicate Phrase.

steps.storyPrompt: Vaani writes two predicate blueprints with identical word counts: (1) "Neha met a famous botanist." (2) "Neha became a famous botanist."
steps.questionPrompt: What is the exact grammatical role of "a famous botanist" in (1) vs. (2)?
options: Subject Complement in (1); Direct Object in (2)
Direct Object in (1); Subject Complement in (2)
acceptedAnswers: Direct Object in (1); Subject Complement in (2)
steps.hint: In (1), Neha and the botanist are TWO different people ('met' is transitive); in (2), Neha IS the botanist ('became' is linking)!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Vaani: "Sharp eye! Transitive 'met' takes a Direct Object (someone else), whereas linking 'became' takes a Subject Complement (renaming Neha)."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Test whether 'Neha = a famous botanist'. If equal, it's a Subject Complement; if two separate people, it's a Direct Object.

feedbackWrongByOption.Direct Object in both sentences: Remember: linking verbs ('is, seem, become') never take objects—they take Complements!

steps.simplerExample: Rohan saw a doctor (Object) vs. Rohan became a doctor (Complement).

steps.stepTitle: Discover: Complex Predicate Patterns (SVOO, SVOC, SVA)
steps.subtopicTitle: SVOO vs. SVOC & Verb Pattern Compatibility
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: Spot the difference between SVOO and SVOC with an Equals Sign (=)! In 'They gave Dev a medal' (Dev ≠ medal → SVOO, two different things). In 'They declared Dev captain' (Dev = captain → SVOC, object + its new label)!
steps.formalDefinition: Predicate phrases follow seven canonical clause patterns: SV, SVA (obligatory adverbial), SVC, SVO, SVOA, SVOO (ditransitive), and SVOC (complex transitive with object complement). In SVOC, an adjective or noun phrase describes or renames the direct object.
steps.simpleExplanation:
Practise telling SVOO from SVOC—a favourite Class IX exam puzzle:
- SVOO (Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object): Can be rewritten with 'to' or 'for': 'She baked Kabir a cake' = 'She baked a cake FOR Kabir' (Kabir ≠ cake).
- SVOC (Verb + Direct Object + Object Complement): Cannot use 'to/for'; instead, you can insert 'to be' between O and C: 'The class elected Priya (to be) monitor', 'The news made everyone (to be) happy', 'He painted the fence green'.
Also remember verb restrictions: 'explain' and 'suggest' do NOT allow *explain me the rule or *suggest me a book — they demand SVO + 'to'-phrase ('explain the rule TO me')!

structurePatterns.formula: SVOO: O1 ≠ O2 (rewritable with to/for) | SVOC: O = C (Noun/Adj describes O)
structurePatterns.sample: Mother bought me a compass (SVOO) vs. The sun turned the leaves brown (SVOC).
Acharya explained the rule to us. (NEVER *explained us the rule)

realLifeExamples.sentence: The judges named Vaani best speaker of the festival.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Predicate = 'named' (V) + 'Vaani' (DO) + 'best speaker of the festival' (Object Complement: Vaani = best speaker).

realLifeExamples.sentence: Could you suggest a good dictionary to our study group?
realLifeExamples.contextNote: 'Suggest' takes Direct Object + 'to'-phrase, never *suggest our group a dictionary.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: Please explain me this predicate pattern, and he suggested us a short break.
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: Please explain this predicate pattern to me, and he suggested a short break to us.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: 'Explain' and 'suggest' do not allow the Indirect Object directly after the verb—place the Direct Object first and add 'to + person'.

exceptions: Ditransitive verbs differ on preposition when flipped: 'give/send/lend/show' take 'to' ('gave the key to me'), while 'buy/make/cook/find' take 'for' ('bought a pen for me').

steps.storyPrompt: Acharya Vidyadhar points to a blueprint: "Good training made the young sprinter unstoppable."
steps.questionPrompt: Which predicate blueprint describes "made the young sprinter unstoppable"?
steps.hint: 'Unstoppable' is an adjective describing what 'the young sprinter' (the Direct Object) became—not a second thing handed to the sprinter!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Acharya Vidyadhar: "Exact blueprint! 'The young sprinter' is the Direct Object, and 'unstoppable' is the Object Complement describing him/her."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Notice 'unstoppable' describes 'the young sprinter' directly (O = C).

feedbackWrongByOption.Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object (: An Indirect + Direct Object requires two nouns, not an adjective like 'unstoppable'!

steps.stepTitle: Checkpoint 4: Fix the Verb Pattern Trap
steps.storyPrompt: Chikoo scribbles a detective memo: "Kindly explain me the riddle, and please put the lantern!"
steps.questionPrompt: Choose the clean sentence fixing BOTH predicate pattern errors:
options: Kindly explain the riddle to me, and please put the lantern on the desk.
Kindly explain me the riddle, and please put the lantern on the desk.
Kindly explain the riddle to me, and please put the lantern.
Kindly explain to me the riddle, and please put carefully the lantern.
acceptedAnswers: Kindly explain the riddle to me, and please put the lantern on the desk.
steps.hint: 'Explain' requires 'explain [something] to [someone]', and 'put' requires a place/destination ('on the desk')!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Maharaj Vakya: "Flawless predicate architecture! 'Explain the riddle to me' and 'put the lantern on the desk' satisfy every requirement of both verbs."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Remember: 'explain + Direct Object + to + person', and 'put + Object + Place'.

feedbackWrongByOption.Kindly explain the riddle to me, and ple: 'Put the lantern' feels cut off—where should it be placed?

steps.simplerExample: Explain the formula to us, and put your bag under the bench.

steps.settingDescription: With every predicate phrase neatly colour-coded into Verb Groups, Objects, Complements, and Adjuncts, Detective Ira locks the blueprint cabinet.

dialogues.line: No more orphan verbs missing their places or objects! Even Chikoo fixed 'explain the riddle to me'.

summaryRules.heading: Predicate Phrase Boundary
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Every clause divides into Subject + Predicate Phrase. The Predicate Phrase contains the verb group plus all objects, complements, and adverbial adjuncts.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: Clause = [Subject NP] + [Verb Group + Required Complements + Optional Adjuncts]
summaryRules.example: The courier [delivered the sealed letter at dawn].

summaryRules.heading: Seven Canonical Predicate Patterns
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Intransitive (SV), Obligatory Adverbial (SVA), Linking (SVC), Monotransitive (SVO), Object+Place (SVOA), Ditransitive (SVOO), and Complex Transitive (SVOC).
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: SVC: S = C | SVOO: O1 ≠ O2 | SVOC: O = C (Adj/Noun)
summaryRules.example: They elected Priya captain (SVOC) vs. They gave Priya a badge (SVOO).

summaryRules.heading: Verbs Requiring Special Predicate Patterns
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Explain, suggest, describe, and introduce take [Direct Object + to + person], never *explain me something. Put and place require a destination/location phrase.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: explain/suggest + Thing + to + Person | put + Thing + Place
summaryRules.example: She suggested a quieter route to the hikers.

memoryAids: Bicycle Rule: Subject = front wheel; Predicate Phrase = everything else (pedals + mandatory rack + optional streamers).
Equals Sign Test: 'They named Dev captain' (Dev = captain → SVOC); 'They gave Dev a pen' (Dev ≠ pen → SVOO).

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: The teacher explained us the theorem and suggested us two exercises.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: The teacher explained the theorem to us and suggested two exercises to us.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: 'Explain' and 'suggest' forbid placing the indirect person right before the direct object.

commonMistakes.correctSentence: She put her umbrella in the corner.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: 'Put' requires an obligatory place adverbial (SVOA) to complete its predicate meaning.

exceptions: When converting SVOO to a prepositional pattern, 'give/lend/send/show' use 'to', whereas 'buy/make/cook/get' use 'for' ('bought a map for me').
textbookNotes: Grounded in Odisha Class IX Ch. 12 (The Predicate Phrase): internal verb patterns, complements, and adjuncts.

questions.questionText: In "The evening breeze cooled the courtyard quickly", which span is the Predicate Phrase?
questions.explanation: Once the subject 'The evening breeze' is separated, the remaining verb group + object + manner adverb ('cooled the courtyard quickly') forms the Predicate Phrase.
distractorRationales: Verb alone omits object and adjunct.
questions.grammarRule: The predicate phrase includes the finite verb together with its objects, complements, and adjuncts.

questions.questionText: Which sentence follows the SVC (Subject + Linking Verb + Subject Complement) pattern?
questions.explanation: In 'The brass bell sounded clear', 'sounded' is a linking verb and 'clear' is an adjective Subject Complement describing the bell.
questions.grammarRule: SVC connects a subject via a linking verb to an adjective or noun describing/renaming the subject.

questions.questionText: In "She placed the glass jar on the wooden shelf before dinner", which element inside the predicate is OPTIONAL (an adjunct that can be omitted cleanly)?
questions.explanation: 'Placed' requires both 'the glass jar' (DO) and 'on the wooden shelf' (obligatory place); only 'before dinner' is an optional time adjunct.
distractorRationales: Main finite verb cannot be removed.
Correct: 'before dinner' is an optional adjunct.
questions.grammarRule: An adjunct adds extra time/manner/place info that can be omitted without making the verb incomplete.

questions.questionText: Identify the sentence built on the SVOC (Verb + Object + Object Complement) pattern:
options: The monsoon rain made the soil fertile.
Detective Ira sent Vaani a telegram.
The children sang folk songs cheerfully.
questions.explanation: In 'made the soil fertile', 'the soil' is the Direct Object and 'fertile' is the Object Complement describing what the soil became.
questions.grammarRule: In SVOC, the final adjective or noun phrase describes or renames the Direct Object.

options: Could you explain me the second clue?
Could you explain the second clue to me?
Could you suggest me a mystery novel?
Could you describe me the suspect?
questions.explanation: 'Explain', 'suggest', and 'describe' do not take an indirect object right after the verb; place the Direct Object first and add 'to + person'.
questions.grammarRule: Use 'explain / suggest / describe + Object + to + Person' (never SVOO).

questions.questionText: Rewrite "Chef Kabir cooked the guests hot jalebis" using a prepositional phrase cleanly:
options: Chef Kabir cooked hot jalebis to the guests.
Chef Kabir cooked hot jalebis for the guests.
Chef Kabir cooked for the guests hot jalebis.
Chef Kabir cooked to the guests hot jalebis.
questions.explanation: Beneficiary verbs like 'cook, bake, buy, make, build' flip to 'Direct Object + FOR + recipient' (not 'to').
questions.grammarRule: Beneficiary SVOO verbs (buy, cook, make, find) alternate with [DO + for + Person].

questions.questionText: Which sentence has a GRAMMATICALLY COMPLETE predicate?
options: The museum lies opposite the botanical garden.
questions.explanation: Verbs of location ('lie', 'live', 'stay') in locative sense and 'put' need an obligatory place phrase; 'hand' needs objects.
distractorRationales: 'Lies' meaning 'is situated' requires a location (unlike 'Never lie').
'Put' requires both an object and a place.
Correct: complete SVA pattern with location.
questions.grammarRule: Some verbs require an obligatory adverbial of place (SVA / SVOA) to be complete.

questions.questionText: In "The school council appointed Ananya chief editor", what is 'chief editor'?
questions.explanation: 'Ananya' is the Direct Object, and 'chief editor' names the role/status Ananya was appointed to (= Object Complement).
distractorRationales: Ananya isn't receiving a separate object.
Correct: noun phrase renaming the Object.
questions.grammarRule: Verbs like appoint, elect, name, call, and make often take [Direct Object + Object Complement].

questions.questionText: Compare: (A) "The watchman remained calm." (B) "The watchman remained at the gate." What are 'calm' and 'at the gate' respectively?
questions.explanation: 'Calm' is an adjective describing the watchman (Subject Complement: SVC); 'at the gate' is a locative phrase telling WHERE he remained (Obligatory Adverbial: SVA).
distractorRationales: Correct: adjective Complement (SVC) vs. place Adverbial (SVA).
'Calm' is obligatory here, not an optional adjunct.
questions.grammarRule: After linking verbs like 'be' and 'remain', adjectives/NPs act as Complements (SVC), whereas place phrases act as Adverbials (SVA).

questions.questionText: Which predicate uses a transitive verb accurately WITHOUT an unnecessary preposition?
options: The committee discussed about the budget.
The students entered into the auditorium quietly.
The committee discussed the budget thoroughly.
We ordered for three plates of dosas.
questions.explanation: 'Discuss', 'enter' (a room/hall), and 'order' (food/goods) are directly transitive and take NO preposition (*discuss about, *enter into a room, *order for).
distractorRationales: Drop 'into' after 'enter' for physical spaces (keep 'enter into' only for agreements).
Correct: direct object 'the budget' with no 'about'.
questions.grammarRule: Do not insert extra prepositions after transitive verbs like discuss, order, enter (a room), and describe.

questions.questionText: Which sentence has ONE subject sharing a COMPOUND predicate (two joined predicate actions)?
options: Vaani wrote the script, and Kabir designed the posters.
Vaani wrote the script and designed the posters.
Because Vaani wrote the script, everyone cheered.
Both Vaani and Kabir applauded loudly.
questions.explanation: 'Vaani' is one single subject performing two coordinated predicate actions: 'wrote the script' AND 'designed the posters'.
distractorRationales: Two separate clauses with two subjects.
Correct: one subject + two joined predicates.
Compound subject ('Vaani and Kabir'), single predicate.
questions.grammarRule: A compound predicate joins two or more verb phrases sharing the same subject.

questions.questionText: Identify the pattern of "Most teenagers find this puzzle challenging":
questions.explanation: 'This puzzle' is the Direct Object, and 'challenging' is the Object Complement describing 'this puzzle' (SVOC).
distractorRationales: 'Challenging' is an adjective, not a second object.
questions.grammarRule: Cognition verbs like 'find, consider, think' often take [Object + Adjective Complement] (SVOC).

questions.questionText: In "The climbers promised to return before sunset", what role does "to return before sunset" play inside the predicate?
questions.explanation: Ask 'Promised WHAT?' → 'to return before sunset'. The to-infinitive phrase acts as the Direct Object of 'promised'.
questions.grammarRule: A to-infinitive or gerund phrase can fill the Direct Object slot inside a predicate.

questions.questionText: Which sentence has ONLY ONE object plus an adjunct (SVOA), rather than two objects (SVOO)?
options: The librarian lent Ravi an encyclopaedia.
Grandmother knitted Arjun a warm muffler.
The postman left a parcel near the porch.
Aunt Maya sent us sweet laddoos.
questions.explanation: In Option C, 'a parcel' is the single Direct Object and 'near the porch' is a Place Adverbial/Adjunct (not an Indirect Object recipient).
distractorRationales: Correct: one DO ('a parcel') + place adverbial ('near the porch').
questions.grammarRule: Check whether the second element is a recipient noun/pronoun (IO) or a prepositional place/time modifier (Adjunct).

questions.storyContext: Detective Ira seals the final blueprint drawer.
questions.questionText: Which sentence matches the SVOO pattern: Subject + Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object?
options: The stars twinkled above the ridge.
Detective Ira handed Chikoo a magnifying glass.
Chikoo painted the signboard bright yellow.
questions.grammarRule: SVOO places the recipient Indirect Object directly before the Direct Object.
